ethernet_send() in subsys/net/l2/ethernet/ethernet.c dropped the caller's reference on an IPv4 packet whenever net_arp_prepare() returned NET_ARP_PKT_REPLACED. That return value is also used when ARP could not queue the packet because every ARP cache entry is already pending. In that case ARP holds no reference of its own, so the original packet was freed before the replacing ARP request was transmitted.

If transmitting the ARP request then failed (a driver send error or an ethernet_fill_header() failure), the error path called net_pkt_ref() on the freed packet. net_if_tx() then called net_pkt_unref() on it again. If the freed net_pkt slab slot was reallocated in between, the stray unref releases a reference owned by an unrelated packet, which is freed while still in use.

An attacker on the local link can drive the ARP cache into the all-pending state. CONFIG_NET_ARP_TABLE_SIZE defaults to 2, so it is enough to elicit replies to a few spoofed, non-responding on-subnet addresses. Reaching the memory corruption also needs a transmit failure the attacker does not directly control and a narrow slab-reuse race. The practical impact is corruption or a crash of the network stack (denial of service).

The OpenThread PSA crypto platform backend in modules/openthread/platform/crypto_psa.c only supported PSA key references. otPlatCryptoAesSetKey() copied aKey->mKeyRef into the AES context unconditionally. On an OpenThread Radio Co-Processor (RCP) build, CONFIG_OPENTHREAD_CRYPTO_PSA does not select CONFIG_OPENTHREAD_PLATFORM_KEY_REF, so OpenThread passes the MAC key as literal bytes and mKeyRef is uninitialized. psa_cipher_encrypt() in otPlatCryptoAesEncrypt() then fails without writing its output, and the error is only caught by an OpenThread assertion that is compiled to a no-op when CONFIG_ASSERT is disabled.

When the RCP handles transmit security in software, AES-CCM* is never keyed. That is the case with Thread 1.2 or later, where CONFIG_OPENTHREAD_MAC_SOFTWARE_TX_SECURITY_ENABLE defaults to y, on a radio driver without IEEE802154_HW_TX_SEC. Every MAC key-id-mode-1 frame goes out with its payload XORed against a single 16-byte pad of stale stack data, reused for every block, and with an unkeyed MIC. CONFIG_OPENTHREAD_CRYPTO_PSA is enabled by default since v4.4.0.

A passive attacker within 802.15.4 radio range can recover the pad from predictable plaintext (for example 6LoWPAN headers) and read the payload of the frames the device transmits. The practical impact is limited. The configuration is not the default (the default Thread version is 1.1), and the same defect makes peers reject every secured data frame, so an affected device cannot exchange data on the network. Received traffic and key distribution are not affected. With CONFIG_ASSERT enabled, the RCP halts on the first secured transmission instead.

The STM32 SMBus driver (drivers/smbus/smbus_stm32.c) implements smbus_block_read() and smbus_block_pcall() by issuing a single i2c_transfer() in which the byte-count byte returned by the peripheral is read directly into the len field of the following i2c_msg. That message then receives data straight into the caller-supplied buffer. Nothing bounds the count, so smbus_stm32_block_read() and smbus_stm32_block_pcall() read up to 255 bytes into a buffer that the SMBus API documents (and the syscall verifiers validate) as holding at most SMBUS_BLOCK_BYTES_MAX (32) bytes.

The count is chosen by the addressed SMBus peripheral. A malicious, counterfeit or faulty device on the bus (for example a removable smart battery, PMBus supply or plug-in module), or anyone able to drive the bus lines, can report a block count above 32 and cause the driver to write up to 223 bytes past the end of the caller's buffer. Callers typically pass a 32-byte stack buffer, as the in-tree smbus block_read shell command does, so the overflow lands on the caller's stack before any caller-side count check can run.

The result is attacker-controlled stack or memory corruption in the context of the calling thread, which can crash the system or potentially be leveraged for code execution. When the call arrives through the smbus_block_read/smbus_block_pcall system calls, the out-of-bounds write happens in supervisor mode beyond the 32-byte region validated for the user thread. The fix receives the block into a driver-local 255-byte buffer and copies it out only when the count is at most SMBUS_BLOCK_BYTES_MAX, returning -ENODATA otherwise.

usbh_req_setup() in subsys/usb/host/usbh_ch9.c returns -ETIMEDOUT as soon as a control request times out, even though the transfer is still in flight. usbh_xfer_dequeue() only requests cancellation, and the host controller driver keeps the transfer and its data buffer until it returns it through the completion callback. Callers such as usbh_req_desc_dev() and usbh_req_desc_cfg() free the buffer (net_buf_unref()) right after usbh_req_setup() returns. Separately, a single global semaphore (ch9_req_sync) with no mutual exclusion lets a late or foreign completion wake the wrong waiter. That waiter then returns early and its caller frees a buffer the controller is still filling.

A malicious USB device attached to a Zephyr USB host port can trigger this during enumeration. It NAKs a GET_DESCRIPTOR request until the 5-second timeout expires, then answers with data around the cancellation, or delays its answer to the next request after leaving a stale semaphore signal. The controller driver (for example the MAX3421E max3421e_hrslt_success() path) then writes device-controlled bytes into the freed net_buf and updates its length.

The result is a use-after-free write into the USB host buffer pool with attacker-chosen contents, which can corrupt buffers that have been reallocated to other transfers, plus a leak of transfer objects. Crashes or memory corruption follow. The fix serializes usbh_req_setup() with a mutex, resets the semaphore before each request, and waits for the driver to return a cancelled transfer before freeing it. Only builds with the experimental CONFIG_USB_HOST_STACK are affected.

The Zephyr TFTP client in subsys/net/lib/tftp/tftp_client.c does not check where the reply to its request comes from. After sending a read or write request to the configured server, send_request() accepts the first UDP datagram that arrives on the client's socket from any address and port. It then calls zsock_connect() to that sender, so the sender becomes the peer for the rest of the transfer. RFC 1350 requires a client to discard datagrams whose source does not match the transfer ID it expects.

A host that can send a UDP datagram to the client's ephemeral port before the real server replies can take over the transfer. It can reply from its own address and does not need to spoof the server. A host on the same network segment that sees the request can do this easily. An off-path attacker must guess the randomized ephemeral port and win the race, which is easier when the server is slow or unreachable. No authentication or user interaction is needed beyond the device starting a transfer through tftp_get() or tftp_put(), for example from an application or the net tftp shell command.

For tftp_get(), the attacker chooses the entire content handed to the application's data callback. For tftp_put(), the whole upload buffer is sent to the attacker. There is no memory corruption. TFTP itself has no authentication, and after the fix an attacker who can spoof the server's IP address can still interfere with a transfer. The fix checks the server's address on the first reply and the full address and port on every later datagram, and drops mismatches without using up the transfer's retries.

The Intel SoC FPGA Agilex5 SoC's static MMU region table in soc/intel/intel_socfpga/agilex5/mmu_regions.c mapped the System Manager peripheral (sysmgr) with MT_P_RW_U_RW. That sets the EL0 access-permission bit in the page-table descriptor, so user mode can read and write the block. The other peripheral windows in the same table, and the same block on the sibling Agilex SoC, are correctly mapped MT_P_RW_U_NA.

On arm64, memory-domain page tables are cloned from the kernel page tables (arch_mem_domain_init()). When CONFIG_USERSPACE is enabled, every user mode thread therefore gets direct load/store access to the System Manager registers, with no partition grant or system call. Any untrusted code running as a user thread can exploit this.

The System Manager controls system-wide state that only the kernel should own: NoC/FPGA-bridge idle requests, SDMMC and EMAC interface configuration, FPGA interface enables and boot scratch registers. A user thread can stall the interconnect or reconfigure peripherals out from under kernel drivers, causing denial of service and integrity loss for the platform, and can read that configuration. This breaks the userspace isolation boundary. Builds without CONFIG_USERSPACE (the default) are not affected. The fix maps the region MT_P_RW_U_NA.

The mount-time recovery scan of the Zephyr Memory Storage (ZMS) key-value store, zms_recover_last_ate() in subsys/kvss/zms/zms.c (subsys/fs/zms/zms.c in older releases), computes the end of the sector's data area incorrectly. Every valid allocation table entry (ATE) reset the data-end bound to the start of the sector, including entries whose value is stored inline (8 bytes or less) and delete entries. When the newest ATE in the active sector is one of these, the scan continues past the ATE area into the payload area and reads stored value bytes as struct zms_ate records.

Any payload slot that passes the ATE check (a CRC8 plus the one-byte sector cycle count) is adopted as the newest entry. zms_init() then sets fs->ate_wra and fs->data_wra from it. The pointers are only this weak check away from data an application may have stored on behalf of a remote party: a BLE-writable device name, provisioned credentials, or configuration received over the network. An attacker who can get about 16 bytes of chosen content persisted in a ZMS value can plant a forged ATE. The forged entry takes effect after the next mount, provided the newest entry in that sector is small or a delete. Random data can also match by chance, which is how the issue was found.

A forged or accidentally matched ATE overrides the stored entry for any chosen id. Its inline data or its offset/len pointer controls what later reads of that key return. The misplaced write pointers also make later writes place ATEs and payloads over other entries' existing data, silently corrupting persistent configuration such as settings values stored in ZMS. The effects are limited to the active flash sector and to what ZMS returns to its callers. No RAM out-of-bounds access was identified.

The Intel SEDI I2C controller driver (drivers/i2c/i2c_sedi.c, used on Intel ISH platforms) waits for each asynchronous transfer with k_sem_take() on a per-controller completion semaphore and a 1 s timeout. When the wait times out, i2c_sedi_api_full_io() aborts the transfer via SEDI_I2C_ABORT_TRANSFER, but if the controller's completion interrupt fires between the timeout expiring and the abort masking interrupts, the callback k_sem_give()s the semaphore and the token is never discarded.

The next transfer on that bus then takes the stale token immediately and returns success (the stale context->err is usually 0) while the controller is still executing it. The HAL interrupt handler (or DMA) keeps copying received bytes into the caller's msgs[i].buf. Since I2C callers typically pass stack buffers, this writes into a stack frame that has already been returned from, and the caller also consumes incomplete data. The desynchronization can persist across later transfers.

Triggering the race requires a transfer to complete just after the 1 s timeout. A device on the I2C bus that controls clock stretching (for example a malicious or tampered peripheral) can steer this timing, and it also supplies the bytes that get written. Exploitation therefore needs physical access to the bus and is timing-dependent. The impact is corruption of kernel or thread stack memory with data the peripheral controls, which can lead to a crash or potentially to code execution. The fix calls k_sem_reset() and clears context->err after the abort, while the transfer mutex is still held.

Several Bluetooth LE Audio services in subsys/bluetooth/audio register global connection and authentication callbacks but assume every connection is LE. When CONFIG_BT_CLASSIC is enabled, the host also invokes these callbacks for BR/EDR connections. For such connections bt_conn_get_dst() returns NULL, and bt_conn_get_info() leaves info.le.dst unset (zero or uninitialized stack data). The CSIP Set Member (csip_disconnected(), handle_csip_disconnect(), handle_csip_auth_complete()), PACS (pacs_auth_pairing_complete(), pacs_security_changed()) and HAS (security_changed(), client_alloc(), client_free()) callbacks then compare or copy a Bluetooth address through that NULL or uninitialized pointer.

A remote device within Bluetooth range can trigger this against a dual-mode device that exposes LE Audio server roles and accepts BR/EDR connections. Opening and closing a BR/EDR ACL link, with no pairing, reaches the CSIP Set Member disconnect path. Completing SSP pairing (for example Just Works) or encryption reaches the PACS and HAS paths.

The impact is denial of service. With CONFIG_ASSERT enabled, the device halts on an assertion (bt_keys_find_addr(), context_alloc()). On platforms that trap NULL or wild reads, it crashes. Otherwise, internal PACS/CSIP/HAS client state is corrupted with bogus addresses. The defects are reads only, and the attacker does not control the address that is dereferenced. The fix adds bt_conn_is_type(conn, BT_CONN_TYPE_LE) checks at the top of the affected callbacks.

The system call verification handlers for smbus_block_read() and smbus_block_pcall() in drivers/smbus/smbus_handlers.c (z_vrfy_smbus_block_read() and z_vrfy_smbus_block_pcall()) validated the device object, the count pointers and (for process call) the send buffer, but never validated the receive buffer (buf / rcv_buf). The call then proceeds into the driver implementation, which runs in supervisor mode and writes the bytes received from the SMBus peripheral through that pointer.

A user-mode thread on a system built with CONFIG_USERSPACE that has been granted access to an SMBus device object can pass an arbitrary address, including kernel data or another thread's memory, as the receive buffer. The driver then writes up to SMBUS_BLOCK_BYTES_MAX (32) bytes of peripheral-supplied data there (the STM32 driver writes as many bytes as the peripheral's length byte announces, up to 255). The address is fully attacker-chosen; the written content comes from the bus and is typically influenceable by the caller through the choice of peripheral and command, or by first writing data to a device that echoes it back.

This breaks the user/kernel isolation boundary: it gives an unprivileged thread a kernel-memory write primitive usable for privilege escalation, or at minimum to corrupt kernel state or crash the system. The fix adds K_SYSCALL_MEMORY_WRITE() checks of the receive buffer for the documented worst case, SMBUS_BLOCK_BYTES_MAX. Systems without CONFIG_USERSPACE are not affected.

Bold pagos en linea WordPress plugin before 3.5.1 contains an improper signature verification vulnerability in the bold_co webhook that allows unauthenticated attackers to forge payment notifications. Attackers can set metadata.reference to begin with 'test' and sign the body with the empty test_secret_key HMAC, marking any unpaid WooCommerce order as paid.

MediaInfoLib before 26.10 contains a divide-by-zero vulnerability in TimeCode::FromString() that allows attackers to crash applications by supplying hour-unit timestamps with fewer than three fractional digits. Attackers can craft a TTML file whose begin or end attribute contains such a timestamp, causing MediaInfo or embedding applications to crash with SIGFPE when opened.

MediaInfoLib before 26.10 contains an out-of-bounds read vulnerability in File_Mpegv::Streams_Fill() that allows attackers to read adjacent memory via an uninitialized chroma_format index. Attackers can craft media files that reach Streams_Fill() before Synched_Init(), crashing MediaInfo or embedding applications and possibly exposing static memory in parser output.

MediaInfoLib before 26.10 contains an out-of-bounds read vulnerability in the VC-1 parser that uses uninitialized AspectRatio, profile and colordiff_format members as unchecked table indices. Attackers can supply a crafted MP4 file that finalizes the VC-1 stream before synchronization, crashing the process and potentially exposing adjacent memory in reported metadata.

MediaInfoLib before 26.10 contains an out-of-bounds read vulnerability in the MPEG-4 Visual parser that allows attackers to read global memory via an uninitialized frame_rate_code index into Mpegv_frame_rate. Attackers can supply a crafted MP4 file that forces stream finalization before parser synchronization, crashing the process or leaking adjacent memory into the reported frame rate.

MediaInfoLib before 26.10 contains an uninitialized pointer dereference vulnerability because the File_Mpeg4_Descriptors constructor leaves the IsCmaf pointer holding stale heap contents. Attackers can supply a crafted MP4 file with an AAC/USAC decoder specific descriptor so File_Usac::Streams_Finish_Conformance_Profile dereferences an invalid address, crashing the application.

MediaInfoLib before 26.10 contains a heap use-after-free vulnerability in the Vorbis setup header parser that allows attackers to trigger reads of freed memory via crafted files. Attackers can supply a crafted Ogg/Vorbis file that makes File_Vorbis::Setup() return early without BS_End_LE(), leaving a stale bitstream pointer that causes crashes or heap disclosure.

Fusion through 1.3.1 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability that allows authenticated users to bypass private-address protection by submitting URLs to the POST /api/feeds/validate endpoint. Attackers can supply a public URL that redirects or links to loopback, private, or link-local addresses, making feedfinder request internal services and leak parsed titles in responses.

Anchr before 3.7.2 contains a stored cross-site scripting vulnerability that allows authenticated users to host HTML files by uploading them through the image upload feature with a spoofed image content type. Attackers can upload an .html file served via GET /api/image/:id from the Anchr origin, running script that steals the victim's localStorage session token for account takeover.

Firefly Pico through 1.12.1 contains an insecure direct object reference vulnerability that allows authenticated users to overwrite other users' profiles by supplying arbitrary profile IDs. Attackers with an access token can send another user's sequential ID to the ProfileController update method, reassigning the profile and destroying the victim's saved settings.

KindleEar 3.0.0 through 3.5.3 contains a remote code execution vulnerability that allows authenticated non-admin users to run Python code by uploading malicious recipes. Attackers can submit crafted recipe source to the /recipe/upload action, which calibre compile_recipe executes via exec() without sandboxing, gaining root code execution in the Docker container and access to password hashes.

Daptin before 0.13.61 contains an incorrect authorization vulnerability that allows authenticated users to overwrite restricted contacts by sending CardDAV PUT requests to existing contacts. Attackers holding address book Update permission can bypass per-contact row permissions in PutAddressObject to modify protected contacts and confirm their existence.

django-appointment before 3.14.2 contains a missing authorization vulnerability that allows authenticated staff members to modify other staff members' appointments by supplying arbitrary appointment IDs. Attackers can send POST requests to /ajax/update_appt_date_time/ with sequential appointment_id values to reschedule appointments, rewriting date, start and end times and reminders.

FLTK through 1.4.5 contains a heap buffer overflow vulnerability in Fl_BMP_Image::load_bmp_() that allows attackers to corrupt heap memory by supplying crafted BMP or ICO files. Attackers can specify very large image dimensions so the 32-bit row and alpha mask pointer offsets wrap, writing file-derived pixel bytes out of bounds to crash applications or possibly execute code.

sdcb Chats 1.10.0 before 1.17.1 contains an incorrect authorization vulnerability in GetAssignedUserDetails that allows assigned non-admin users to read other users' per-user MCP headers. Attackers can request the assigned-user-details endpoint to obtain bearer tokens in CustomHeaders and impersonate other users against the downstream MCP server.

MyBibliotheca 3.0.0 before 3.0.4 contains an insecure direct object reference vulnerability that allows authenticated users to modify or delete other users' books via /api/v1/books/<book_id>. Attackers can obtain book UUIDs from recently added books across all owners, then send PUT or DELETE requests to rename, alter, or permanently delete them.

KindleEar 3.0.0 through 3.5.3 contains an insecure direct object reference vulnerability in application/view/subscribe.py that allows authenticated users to access other users' records by id without ownership checks. Attackers can enumerate sequential recipe ids to read recipe source containing credentials, delete recipes and custom RSS feeds, and overwrite saved site logins.

Tabbycat 2.9.0 through 2.12.1 contains an incorrect authorization vulnerability in TournamentViewSet that allows unauthenticated attackers to gain write access because PerTournamentPermissionRequired returns True for views lacking a tournament attribute. Attackers can send POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE requests to /api/v1/tournaments to create, modify or delete tournaments, cascading deletion to teams and speakers.

Automura for Gravity Forms – Webhooks & REST API for Automation before 1.0.1 contains a reflected cross-site scripting vulnerability in Rest_Admin::serve_file() on the global rest_pre_serve_request filter. Unauthenticated attackers can craft REST links setting automura_gf_file to script HTML and automura_gf_file_type to text/html, executing JavaScript with a victim administrator's session.

odf-kit is a TypeScript and JavaScript library for working with OpenDocument Format files. In versions 0.9.8 through 0.14.1, the odsToHtml() renderer inserts document-controlled cell formatting and row height values into HTML style attributes without escaping them. An attacker can craft an ODS file that injects arbitrary HTML attributes or elements, allowing JavaScript execution in the host page's origin when an application inserts the converted output as HTML. This issue is fixed in version 0.14.2.

GFI HelpDesk before 4.99.13 contains an SQL injection vulnerability in the archiver export feature that allows authenticated attackers with administrator privileges to execute arbitrary SQL queries by supplying crafted itemid[] array values to /admin/index.php?/archiver/Manager/ExportAll. The Controller_Manager.ExportAll() method joins the itemid values with implode() and GetWhere() concatenates them into an IN() clause without sanitization or parameterization, and DumpTables() executes the resulting query against each ticket-related table, allowing attackers to read or modify database contents.

GFI HelpDesk before 4.99.13 contains an SQL injection vulnerability in the staff group management feature that allows authenticated attackers with administrator privileges to execute arbitrary SQL queries by supplying a crafted title parameter to /admin/index.php?/Base/StaffGroup/InsertSubmit. The Controller_StaffGroup.RunChecks() method concatenates the unsanitized title value directly into a duplicate name lookup query against the staffgroup table, allowing attackers to read or modify database contents.

In SignalError of logical_link.cc, there is a possible use after free due to an error callback that can destroy the object while its channel list is still being iterated. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

In DataElement::Read of data_element.cc, there is a possible stack exhaustion due to unbounded recursion. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) denial of service with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

In ServiceSearchResponse::GetPDU of pdu.cc, there is a possible crash due to an incorrect size calculation. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) denial of service with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

In HandleRxPacket of logical_link.cc, there is a possible resource exhaustion due to a missing limit on packets buffered for channels that are never opened. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) denial of service with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

In Phase2SecureConnections::OnPeerPublicKey of phase_2_secure_connections.cc, there is a possible way to learn the passkey used during pairing due to an incomplete check for a reflected public key. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is needed for exploitation.

In OnRxLeCreditBasedConnectionRequest of le_dynamic_channel.cc, there is a possible assertion failure due to improper input validation. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) denial of service with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

In BluetoothSetupImpl::OnAudioSourceConnectChanged of bluetooth_setup_impl.cc, there is a possible way for an unauthenticated nearby Bluetooth device to be saved as the audio output device due to a logic error in the code. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) escalation of privilege with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

In reconnect.shard.cml, there is a possible way to turn off the camera streaming and microphone mute indicator LEDs due to an unnecessary hardware capability grant. This could lead to local escalation of privilege with User execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

In StartA2dpOffload of a2dp_offload_manager.cc, there is a possible use after free due to a stored callback that is not cleared when the link it refers to is destroyed. This could lead to remote (proximal/adjacent) code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

In ServerSessionBroker of server_session_broker.cc, there is a possible use after free due to a race condition. This could lead to remote code execution with no additional execution privileges needed. User interaction is not needed for exploitation.

The AIL Framework web application contains a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in its dashboard templates. In the home dashboard (dashboard.html), the hunter trackers dashboard (trackers_dashboard.html), and the objects dashboard (objs_dashboard.html), object global identifiers (GIDs) derived from filenames or message IDs were interpolated directly into inline JavaScript event handler attributes (onmouseenter/onmouseleave) within HTML anchor tags. Because the GID value was placed inside a single-quoted JavaScript string literal within an HTML attribute, an attacker who could control the GID value (for example, by crafting a filename or message ID containing a single quote) could break out of the string context and inject arbitrary JavaScript code that would execute in the context of any user viewing the dashboard.

Additionally, in dynamically generated JavaScript code within the same templates, object identifiers were concatenated into HTML strings and inline event handler registrations without sufficient encoding, presenting a similar injection surface. The AJAX tooltip lookup also concatenated the raw GID into a URL without encoding, which could be leveraged for further manipulation.

The vulnerability requires that an attacker be able to influence the GID value stored in the application (e.g., through a file upload or message creation with a crafted name) and that a victim subsequently visits one of the affected dashboard pages and hovers over the affected object link. Successful exploitation allows execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the victim's browser session, potentially leading to session hijacking, data exfiltration, or unauthorized actions performed on behalf of the victim.

pgjdbc, the PostgreSQL JDBC Driver, does not refuse a NUL character in a startup parameter. The StartupMessage is a list of NUL-terminated strings, so a NUL in the database name, user, currentSchema, options or ApplicationName adds further parameters. %00 in a URL decodes to a NUL. Someone who controls part of the URL or a property can choose another login role or add replication=database, although the connection still has to pass the authentication of that role. On a server that trusts the client, the attacker can log in as any role. All versions before 42.7.15 are affected, and 42.7.15 fixes the problem.

pgjdbc, the PostgreSQL JDBC Driver, cuts the weight and scale of a BigDecimal to 16 bits when it sends the value in binary, which is the default. The server then stores a different number without an error. For example 999999.99e-262144 is stored as 999999.99, so a tiny value can pass a range check and be stored as a large one. The driver also computes 10 to the power of the scale first, so a short value such as 1e-200000000 keeps a thread busy for minutes. Versions 42.3.0 through 42.7.14 are affected, and 42.7.15 fixes the problem.

pgjdbc, the PostgreSQL JDBC Driver, does not check the token state that GSSContext.unwrap() reports on a GSS-encrypted connection. An attacker on the network path can replay an earlier server packet from the same connection, and the driver accepts it as the answer to the current query. The driver also shares one MessageProp between reading and writing. One integrity-only packet from the server then makes the driver send later SQL and parameters without encryption. Only connections with gssEncMode=prefer or require that start GSS encryption are affected. Versions 42.2.15 through 42.7.14 are affected, and 42.7.15 fixes the problem.

pgjdbc, the PostgreSQL JDBC Driver, does not enforce TLS for some settings that ask for it. When sslmode is not set, an ssl value such as 1, on, yes or verify-full gives sslmode=prefer, or no TLS before 42.2.5. A service given in the Properties instead of the URL is ignored, so the sslmode of its pg_service.conf entry is lost. BaseDataSource.setUrl() keeps an sslmode, channelBinding or gssEncMode that was set before it. An attacker on the network path can then read and change the traffic. Versions 9.4.1208 through 42.7.14 are affected, and 42.7.15 fixes the problem.

pgjdbc, the PostgreSQL JDBC Driver, uses unqualified operators and functions in the catalog queries of DatabaseMetaData, ResultSetMetaData and TypeInfoCache. A role with CREATE on a schema of the application's search_path can add an operator with an exact type match, and the server runs it with the privileges of the application's role. TypeInfoCache also resolves an unqualified type name such as interval by its own ranking. A domain with that name in another schema, even the temporary schema of another session, can be used instead, and its CHECK runs in the application's session. All versions before 42.7.15 are affected, and 42.7.15 fixes the problem.

pgjdbc, the PostgreSQL JDBC Driver, does not close the connection when an unchecked exception interrupts a request. Part of a Bind message stays in the send buffer, and the server reads the bytes that follow as the rest of it. The bytes of a value uploaded later on the same connection can then run as a SQL command. Since 42.6.0 a setBinaryStream() value without a length that is executed again throws such an exception, as does the driver's own retry after SQLState 0A000 or 26000. An application stream that throws an unchecked exception has the same effect in all versions. All versions before 42.7.15 are affected, and 42.7.15 fixes the problem.

pgjdbc, the PostgreSQL JDBC Driver, can quote a string parameter for the wrong value of standard_conforming_strings when preferQueryMode=simple is set. A statement, trigger or configuration reload can turn the setting off during a session. A parameter value with a backslash and a quote then ends the literal, and the rest of the value runs as SQL. Before 42.7.6 any session with the setting off was affected. The statement cache can also reuse a parse made under the other setting. With allowEncodingChanges=true and the EUC_JP or SJIS client encoding, the yen sign acts as a backslash. All versions before 42.7.15 are affected, and 42.7.15 fixes the problem.

pgjdbc, the PostgreSQL JDBC Driver, misreads some quoted text in its query parser. A `}` inside a literal ends a JDBC escape such as `{ts}`, and the rest of the literal is translated as SQL. A dollar quote whose tag has a non-ASCII symbol or space is not recognized. An `E''` string with a doubled quote is scanned as a standard string. `{fn right}` and `{fn timestampdiff}` with a negative argument produce a `--` comment. In each case text that the application quoted correctly can run as SQL with the privileges of the application's database role. All versions before 42.7.15 are affected, and 42.7.15 fixes the problem.

XO (Xen Orchestra) is a solution to visualize, manage, backup and delegate your XCP-ng (or XenServer) infrastructure. Prior to 6.9.2 and 6.10.1, REST cookie parsing turns authenticationToken=j:%7B%7D into {}. REST authentication passes that object to the XO token provider without requiring a string. The token collection treats {} as an unfiltered lookup and returns its first token; the provider authenticates as that token's owner if it is unexpired. The authenticated /rest/v0/users/me/authentication_tokens route then returns reusable login token IDs. This vulnerability is actively exploited in the wild. This vulnerability is fixed in 6.9.2 and 6.10.1.
